title: What makes a genius?
summary: Stuff You Should Know episode examining what makes a genius. The hosts trace the Greco-Roman original meaning of "genius" (natural enthusiasm for an activity), Francis Galton's shift to intellect and eugenics, and why genius is hard to quantify. They adopt Tracy V. Wilson's definition of genius as an extraordinarily intelligent person who breaks new ground with discoveries, inventions, or works of art. They discuss William James Sidis as a prodigy who was not a genius by that definition, brain research (cerebral cortex, gray matter, Einstein's parietal lobe, cortical thickness studies), IQ tests and their history and biases (Katherine Morris Cox, Galton, Binet), Sternberg's triarchic theory, Cattell's fluid and crystallized intelligence, Gardner's multiple intelligences, the link between giftedness and social awkwardness, creativity and latent inhibition, Simonton's citation-based measures, Ericsson's ten-thousand-hour practice rule and Gladwell, David Galenson's conceptual versus experimental innovators, and a list of commonly named geniuses. The episode closes with listener mail from a female truck driver and an eleven-year-old listener named Sam.

segments.title: Opening banter and the word genius
segments.summary: The hosts joke around and then discuss how 'genius' was originally used in the Greco-Roman era to mean a natural enthusiasm or inclination toward an activity, rather than raw ability.

segments.title: Galton, eugenics and quantifying genius
segments.summary: Francis Galton first tied genius to intellect, leading to the idea that genius can be quantified through IQ tests. The hosts argue genius is subjective and hard to study, and adopt Tracy V. Wilson's definition: an extraordinarily intelligent person who breaks new ground with discoveries, inventions, or art.

segments.title: William James Sidis and the prodigy distinction
segments.summary: The hosts describe William James Sidis, who reportedly had a very high IQ, learned languages early, and graduated from Harvard young, but then took menial jobs and contributed no creative work, so he would not count as a genius under the adopted definition. They also discuss how many geniuses MENSA membership implies and why that estimate is flawed.

segments.title: Brain structure and intelligence
segments.summary: The hosts cover the cerebral cortex and brain stem, the difficulty of studying the living brain with MRI, a 2004 UC Irvine study linking gray matter volume to intelligence, and Einstein's brain, which had an unusually narrow parietal lobe fissure. A 2006 Nature study linked faster cortical thickening in youth to higher IQ.

segments.title: History of IQ tests
segments.summary: Katherine Morris Cox's 1926 book on the early mental traits of 301 great minds ranked Johann Gutenberg highest. IQ tests were first used to identify mental handicaps, then adapted to find gifted children, and the Stanford-Binet test came from Binet's and Stanford psychologists' work. The hosts discuss the scoring scale and the unproven 140 threshold for genius.

segments.title: Biases and limits of standardized tests
segments.summary: The hosts argue standardized tests cannot measure everything and can be biased; an example question about where to buy milk illustrates cultural and socioeconomic bias. They note geniuses don't necessarily score well on these tests.

segments.title: Theories of intelligence: Sternberg, Cattell, Gardner
segments.summary: The hosts review Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory (creative, analytical, practical intelligence), Raymond Cattell's fluid, crystallized, and visual-spatial intelligence, and Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences. They note critics disagree with each theory.

segments.title: Social awkwardness, creativity and measuring genius output
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the stereotype of quirky geniuses, a Purdue study on gifted students being bullied, a Stanford twenty-year study finding negative correlation between IQ and social adjustment, and latent inhibition in creative people. They cover Dean Keith Simonton's citation-based measures, Ericsson's ten-year or ten-thousand-hour practice rule, Gladwell, and David Galenson's conceptual versus experimental innovators.

segments.title: Famous geniuses list and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts react to a ranked list of historical geniuses including Tesla, da Vinci, Newton, Hawking, Michelangelo, Archimedes, and Einstein, and conclude that genius is subjective, comparing it to pornography: hard to define but recognizable. They point listeners to related articles and series on painters.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts plug their Facebook page and Twitter account, then read listener mail from a female truck driver who corrects their view of truckers and from eleven-year-old Sam, who asks about phrases and riot control. The episode ends with a sponsor line.
